items.readable_text:
Content:
We know that when a transversal crosses two parallel lines, a set of [MATH: 8] interesting angles are formed, some of which are congruent and others of which are supplementary.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/19f78e22c6a522853d0877f813cc3df8]

Content:
The reverse is also true: when certain angles formed by a transversal are congruent or supplementary, then the two lines that the transversal crosses must be parallel.

Content:
More precisely, two lines are parallel if they are crossed by a transversal such that:

Content:
- the corresponding angles are congruent:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/40b6753005d84a4a47ecb0c9385aba98]

Content:
- or, the alternate (interior or exterior) angles are congruent

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/d8e0101446146cd12af7712a89c541a1]

Content:
- or, the consecutive (interior or exterior) angles are supplementary.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b052cd8fba902e88223d1b7046f41fa9]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/21d3186455914c05ff155e0053aaeed3]

Content:
If at least one pair of angles satisfies the conditions above, then the two lines are parallel.

Content:
Watch out: When two lines are parallel, we also know that the vertical angles are congruent and the adjacent are supplementary. These, however, are true conditions for any pair of crossing lines, and therefore cannot be used as criteria for parallel lines.

Given the lines [MATH: \overset{\longleftrightarrow}{AB},\, \overset{\longleftrightarrow}{CD},] and [MATH: \overset{\longleftrightarrow}{PS}] shown above, for which value of [MATH: x] is [MATH: \overset{\longleftrightarrow}{AB} \parallel \overset{\longleftrightarrow}{CD}?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, notice that [MATH: \angle PQA] and [MATH: \angle PQB] are supplementary angles. So, we have:

[MATH: m∠PQB + m∠PQA|= 180^{∘}; m∠PQB + 61^{∘}|= 180^{∘}; m∠PQB|= 119^{∘}]

The lines [MATH: \overset{\longleftrightarrow}{AB}] and [MATH: \overset{\longleftrightarrow}{CD}] are cut by the transversal [MATH: \overset{\longleftrightarrow}{PS}.]

The angles [MATH: \angle PQB] and [MATH: \angle QRD] are corresponding angles. To have parallel lines, the corresponding angles must be congruent.

To have [MATH: \overset{\longleftrightarrow}{AB} \parallel \overset{\longleftrightarrow}{CD},] we need [MATH: \angle PQB\cong\angle QRD.] So, these two angles must have the same measure:

[MATH: m∠PQB|= m∠QRD; 119^{∘}|= 11x − 2^{∘}; 121^{∘}|= 11x; 11^{∘}|= x]

Therefore, [MATH: x = 11^\circ.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
We know that when a transversal crosses two parallel lines, a set of [MATH: 8] interesting angles are formed, some of which are congruent and others of which are supplementary.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/19f78e22c6a522853d0877f813cc3df8]

Content:
The reverse is also true: when certain angles formed by a transversal are congruent or supplementary, then the two lines that the transversal crosses must be parallel.

Content:
More precisely, two lines are parallel if they are crossed by a transversal such that:

Content:
- the corresponding angles are congruent:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/40b6753005d84a4a47ecb0c9385aba98]

- or, the alternate (interior or exterior) angles are congruent

Graphic:

- or, the consecutive (interior or exterior) angles are supplementary.

[IMG: /graphics/21d3186455914c05ff155e0053aaeed3]

If at least one pair of angles satisfies the conditions above, then the two lines are parallel.

Content:
